slides.title: Ethereum’s and Telegram’s founders want privacy built into the apps people already use
paragraphs: Ethereum’s and Telegram’s founders want privacy built into the apps people already use
Buterin wants privacy built into Ethereum itself, and Durov would rather leave a market than weaken Telegram’s encryption.
Vitalik Buterin
Co-founder
Ethereum
“Privacy is not about standing apart. It’s about standing together.” “Why I support privacy”, Buterin’s blog, 14 April 2025
Why privacy matters
Control over information is power, so privacy protects decentralisation, personal freedom and institutions such as the secret ballot.
What he proposes
Build privacy into Ethereum itself, covering payments, app activity, what users look up and their network identity.
What is missing today
Ethereum transactions are still public by default, and most of the plan needs wallets and apps to build it.
Pavel Durov
Founder and CEO
Telegram, over 1B monthly users
“Telegram would rather exit a market than undermine encryption with backdoors and violate basic human rights.” Post on Durov’s Telegram channel, 21 April 2025
Why privacy matters
Encryption protects everyday communication and personal safety, and any access built for authorities is also available to attackers.
What he proposes
Keep Telegram’s encryption free of government backdoors, even if Telegram has to leave a country to do it.
What is missing today
Telegram’s default chats are not end-to-end encrypted; only its opt-in Secret Chats are.
Implication Privacy that plugs into the wallets and apps people already use has the clearest path to mainstream adoption.

charts.description: From enforcement to infrastructure: privacy policy and builder milestones, 2022 to 2026
labels: Tornado Cash under sanctions for 31 months
Court rules its code is not property

details.label: 31 months under sanctions
details.description: Tornado Cash stayed on the US sanctions list from 8 August 2022 until 21 March 2025. For that period any US person who used it risked breaking sanctions law, which pushed developers and companies away from onchain privacy tools.
details.source: US Treasury; Van Loon v. Treasury

details.label: US Treasury sanctions Tornado Cash
details.description: Tornado Cash is an Ethereum mixer: users deposit into a shared pool and withdraw to a fresh address, breaking the public link between sender and recipient. On 8 August 2022 the US Treasury’s sanctions office (OFAC) blacklisted its smart contracts, saying it had laundered more than $7B since 2019, including $455M stolen by North Korea’s Lazarus Group.

details.label: Court rules code is not property
details.description: In Van Loon v. Department of the Treasury, decided 26 November 2024, the Fifth Circuit appeals court held that Tornado Cash’s immutable smart contracts are not property that can be sanctioned, because nobody owns or controls them. It put ownerless privacy code outside sanctions law at the appellate level.
details.source: US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, 26 November 2024

details.label: Buterin and Durov
details.description: On 11 April 2025 Buterin proposed making privacy part of Ethereum’s core design, covering payments, app activity, chain reads and network-level anonymity. On 21 April Durov said Telegram would leave a market rather than build encryption backdoors for authorities. Two founders with very large user bases put privacy at the centre of their products.
details.source: Buterin, 11 April 2025; Durov’s Telegram channel, 21 April 2025

details.label: USAD and the Privacy Cluster
details.description: On 1 October 2025 Paxos Labs and Aleo announced USAD, a US dollar stablecoin whose balances and transfers are private by default. On 9 October the Ethereum Foundation formed a Privacy Cluster of 47 researchers, engineers and cryptographers to make privacy a first-class property of Ethereum.
details.source: Paxos Labs and Aleo, 1 October 2025; The Block, 9 October 2025

details.label: a16z: privacy is crypto’s moat
details.description: a16z crypto’s Ali Yahya argued that privacy will be the strongest moat for blockchains: “bridging tokens is easy, bridging secrets is hard”. A chain that holds users’ private state is harder to leave than one that holds only public balances, which favours privacy networks that gain users early.

details.label: Sui confidential transfers enter public beta
details.description: On 8 June 2026 the Sui Foundation opened confidential transfers in public beta on Devnet. Balances and amounts are hidden onchain while sender and receiver stay visible; issuers opt their tokens in and set who can access data for compliance. Bridge is exploring it for stablecoin payments, and TRM Labs and Merkle Science for monitoring. Testnet is targeted for later in 2026, with no mainnet date.

details.label: Venice Series A
details.description: Venice, the private AI platform behind VVV, raised a $65M Series A at a $1B valuation led by Dragonfly. It reported 3.5M registered users and a $100M annualised revenue run rate in August 2026 (company-reported).
details.source: TechCrunch via AI Weekly, 1 July 2026; Erik Voorhees via Phemex, August 2026

details.label: ZEC passes $20B as its ETF fills
details.description: Grayscale’s Zcash ETF (ZCSH) began trading on NYSE Arca on 25 August 2026 and held $463.2M by 7 September, giving investors with ordinary brokerage accounts regulated exposure to a privacy coin. On that same day ZEC reached $1,249, taking its market value to about $20.4B and making it the ninth-largest crypto asset, ahead of Hyperliquid.
details.source: Grayscale; NYSE Arca, 25 August to 7 September 2026; Bitcoin.com News and Cointelegraph, 7 September 2026, citing CoinGecko

details.label: US Treasury lifts the sanctions
details.description: The US Treasury removed Tornado Cash from the sanctions list on 21 March 2025, so US users could interact with it again. Developer liability is still open: in August 2025 a jury convicted developer Roman Storm of conspiring to run an unlicensed money-transmitting business and deadlocked on laundering and sanctions charges, which face retrial on 26 April 2027.

details.label: GENIUS Act
details.description: The Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for US Stablecoins Act, signed on 18 July 2025, is the first US federal law for payment stablecoins, setting rules for reserves, licensing and redemption. It gives banks and payment companies a legal route onto public chains, bringing payroll and supplier flows that companies normally keep confidential.

slides.title: Sui is building private stablecoin payments that issuers and auditors can still see into
paragraphs: Sui is building private stablecoin payments that issuers and auditors can still see into
Sui’s confidential transfers hide amounts and balances but keep senders, receivers and an issuer-chosen auditor in view, the controlled privacy that banks and payment firms say they need.

What it does Stablecoin issuers can switch on a confidential mode, so amounts and balances are encrypted onchain while addresses stay public and an auditor chosen by the issuer can read each transfer.
Where it stands In public beta on Sui’s Devnet since June 2026, with mainnet targeted for Q4 2026. The code is open source but not yet audited.

Who is building with it Bridge is exploring it as a stablecoin issuer, and TRM Labs and Merkle Science are testing compliance tools. It builds on fee-free stablecoin transfers that went live on Sui in May 2026.
What to watch Whether it reaches mainnet on schedule, whether a large issuer such as Bridge switches it on, and whether stablecoins on Sui grow from about $470M today.

details.description: On Sui, each confidential transfer carries a copy of the amount that only the issuer’s chosen auditor can decrypt, with an onchain proof that it matches. Zcash shielded amounts are visible only to the parties, or to anyone they share a viewing key with.

slides.title: Stablecoin payments could pay about $2B a year for privacy, over half of it from businesses
paragraphs: Stablecoin payments could pay about $2B a year for privacy, over half of it from businesses

Of about $62T moved by stablecoins in 2025, 93% was bots and intermediary hops, and within the $4.2T of real activity, trading and exchange flows are seven times larger than payments, but payments are where a 0.5% privacy fee is plausible.
Businesses are the larger prize at about $1.1B a year, but consumer transfers are where stablecoins are already used most, so consumer privacy wallets may find paying users first.
The $2.7T of trading and exchange flows is a second, lower-fee market, where privacy hides positions from copy-traders and front-running bots, and which Umbra’s private swaps already serve.
These fees go to whoever processes private stablecoin flows, so Zcash and Monero holders only benefit if that activity moves onto their chains.

slides.title: Privacy as money is worth $32B, about 14 times all other privacy tokens combined
paragraphs: Privacy as money is worth $32B, about 14 times all other privacy tokens combined
Zcash and Monero, held as private money, are worth about $32B together, while the nine other tokens in this report, from apps to newer chains, total about $2.3B, led by Venice at $1.2B.
Like Bitcoin, Zcash and Monero are valued as money to hold rather than on fees, while the app tokens’ value depends on their products growing and linking that use to the token.
CoinGecko’s privacy coins category, the market’s usual benchmark, is worth about $32.1B, and Zcash and Monero make up 98% of it.

Holding privately is still a minority habit, with about 70% of ZEC in transparent addresses, yet at $20.9B ZEC is worth about 1.8 times Monero, so its price assumes private use keeps growing.

hover_details.label: NOCK

hover_details.description: Pearl miners run the matrix maths used in AI inference, so the same GPU work can serve a customer and compete for PRL block rewards. Its zero-knowledge mining proofs are designed to verify the work without revealing the matrices, which can hold model weights or user data. PRL transfers themselves are not shielded, and private, verifiable inference for customers is being developed with Attestable.

slides.title: Umbra brings private transfers and swaps to Solana, built on Arcium
paragraphs: Umbra brings private transfers and swaps to Solana, built on Arcium
Users deposit Solana tokens into a private balance that hides who paid whom and how much, while protocol fees build a treasury that UMBRA holders direct through MetaDAO votes.

What to watch Whether deposits grow from a small base, whether more apps follow Streamflow in building on Umbra, and how the DAO chooses to use its fee income.

details.label: Deposit
details.description: Moving tokens from a Solana wallet into Umbra is public: anyone can see the wallet, the token and the amount.

details.description: Inside Umbra, balances are held privately. The public record shows only the program’s total holdings. The wallet runs on Arcium’s encrypted execution network on Solana.

details.label: Send or withdraw
details.description: A private send hides the sender, recipient, amount and token; a relayer submits it. A withdrawal to any Solana address shows the destination, token and amount, but not which balance paid for it.

details.label: What stays private
details.description: Deposits are public and linked to the depositing wallet. Transfers inside Umbra hide sender, recipient, amount and token. Withdrawals show destination, token and amount, so withdrawing the exact amount just deposited can still link the two.

details.label: Protocol fee
details.description: Each private transaction commits a protocol fee in the token used. Governance sets the rate per token, and Umbra’s protocol documentation caps any default at 5%. Relayers can also receive a public tip.
details.source: Umbra documentation, fee model and fee collection

details.label: Treasury
details.description: Protocol fees are paid to a treasury payout account that only a timelocked governance proposal can set. Nothing in the documentation buys back UMBRA or pays fees to holders.

details.label: UMBRA holders
details.description: Umbra launched through MetaDAO, where proposals pass or fail according to markets that trade on their expected effect on the token price. Holders therefore control how the treasury is used, but receive no automatic share of fees.

paragraphs: Nockchain mines with zero-knowledge proofs and plans private NOCK transfers for 2027

What it does Money on a chain whose miners produce zero-knowledge proofs instead of hashes. Since August, miners can also win blocks doing the matrix maths used in AI inference.

What to watch Whether the ZK opcode, privacy pool and private apps ship on their 2027 dates, and whether paid AI demand grows beyond the founder’s own company.

details.label: The connection
details.description: Wallets send requests to network nodes over the internet, so an observer at an internet exchange or provider router can link a wallet address to an IP address from traffic timing. The study’s authors name Tor or VPNs as possible defences; mixnets such as Nym and decentralised VPNs such as URnetwork also hide where traffic comes from.
details.source: Wang et al., Time Tells All, arXiv:2508.21440v1; Nym and URnetwork documentation

details.label: Entry and exit
details.description: Nullmask, Umbra and Zcash all keep balances and transfers private inside their pools, but moving funds in or out is public. Umbra’s documentation warns that withdrawing the exact amount just deposited can link the two, and Nullmask’s Waves withdrawals split an exit into parts.
details.source: Nullmask documentation, privacy and fees; Umbra documentation, checked 20 October 2026

details.label: The operator
details.description: Nullmask’s documentation says its servers hold users’ account keys and that it protects against outside observers, not the operator. Venice’s default Private mode relies on a contractual promise, while its TEE and end-to-end encrypted modes and Umbra’s computation on Arcium are designed so the operator cannot read the data.
details.source: Nullmask documentation, privacy; venice.ai/privacy; The Block, 27 March 2026

paragraphs: URnetwork is a privacy network, and its VPN is the first app built on it

Ordinary people lend their devices to carry encrypted traffic, apps such as the ur.io VPN sell access to that network, and the UR (SN25) subnet on Bittensor tests it and rewards the people who run it.

What it does A peer-to-peer network that relays encrypted traffic through community devices, so no single company or node sees the whole path. The ur.io VPN, free with paid plans, is the first app selling access to it.
Traction About 350K monthly users (team-reported) and 92,204 providers in 101 countries listed on its site today.
The UR (SN25) token The token of Bittensor subnet 25, worth about $9.7M. Its emissions pay providers and validators, and operators are designed to deposit UR against the traffic they sell.
What to watch Whether a second app goes live on the network, whether operator deposits are switched on so that usage creates demand for the token, and whether paid users grow.

slides.title: UR (SN25)’s operator roadmap extends from consumer VPNs into enterprise and AI
paragraphs: UR (SN25)’s operator roadmap extends from consumer VPNs into enterprise and AI
With ur.io already live and enterprise and AI programmes still in research, the peer figures illustrate market scale rather than forecast UR (SN25) revenue.
Operators can share the miner fleet, although additional traffic still creates operating costs.
AI agents are routinely blocked by bot controls and data-centre IP detection, and residential routes are what let them reach the open web.
If these programmes become paying operators, their traffic could create UR (SN25) demand once deposits are priced.
